transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, what brings me in... I've been having these really strange moments lately. Like, I'll just be sitting in my office—I'm a tax preparer, you see, and we're starting to gear up for the busy season. It's always a massive headache this time of year. Just the other day, this client, Bob, brings in a literal grocery bag full of crumpled gas station receipts and diner napkins. I keep telling him, "Bob, I can't write off your morning donuts," but he never listens, just dumps them on my desk every single year and expects me to perform miracles. 

But anyway, what I was saying... I'll be sitting there at the desk, or even just at home in my own house, and suddenly everything feels completely unreal. It's like I'm watching myself from across the room instead of actually being there. Just looking at this guy sitting at a desk, like it's a movie or something. It's really unsettling. I don't know, maybe Bob's receipts are finally getting to me, but it's just a very bizarre feeling to not feel like you're in your own body.
Have you experienced any other sensations where things around you felt unreal, distorted, or emotionally distant, beyond just feeling like you're watching yourself from outside your body?

No, not really. I mean, it's mostly just that weird out-of-body thing I mentioned. Things around me don't look distorted or anything like that. The desk is still a desk, the receipts are still receipts... God, so many receipts. Speaking of which, you wouldn't believe the ink they use on those thermal paper rolls nowadays. It fades so fast! If a client waits six months to bring it in, it's just a blank white strip. I had to buy this special magnifying glass with an LED light just to make out the numbers for Mrs. Gable's catering business. She runs this lovely little operation, makes the best Swedish meatballs you've ever had, but her record-keeping is just atrocious. She keeps everything in shoe boxes. Actual shoe boxes! I told her, "Martha, they sell file folders at the dollar store," but she says she likes the smell of the leather... What were we talking about? Oh, right, the unreal feeling. No, it's really just that feeling of watching myself. Everything else looks normal, just... I'm not in it, you know?
Have you ever felt like the world around you seemed unreal or like you were in a dream, even when you weren't feeling detached from your body?

No, no, nothing like that. The world doesn't feel like a dream, it's just that one thing I told you about. The room is totally normal, it's just me that feels... off. Honestly, sometimes I wish I was in a dream, especially when I'm dealing with the IRS hold music. Have you ever had to call them? It's this awful, tinny classical music that loops every thirty seconds. I had to sit on hold for two hours last Tuesday trying to sort out a penalty abatement for this guy, Gary. Gary runs a small landscaping company, nice guy, but he tried to claim his dog's food as a security expense because the dog barks at the mailman. I told him, "Gary, unless that golden retriever has a badge and a W-2, the IRS isn't going to buy it." He argued with me for twenty minutes about how loud the dog's bark is. But anyway, yeah, the world feels completely real. Too real, sometimes, especially when Gary's dog is barking in the background of our calls. But no dream-like feelings, no.
Have you ever felt like the world around you seemed unreal, distant, or detached, even when you weren't experiencing that out-of-body sensation?

I feel like we might be going in circles a bit, Doc. Like I just mentioned, no, the world doesn't feel distant or detached at all. It's really just that one weird out-of-body thing with myself. Everything else is completely normal. 

Though, if you want to talk about being detached from reality, you really ought to sit in on some of my appointments with the younger clients. The cryptocurrency guys? Good lord. I had this kid, maybe 23, come in last week. He bought some digital coin named after a cartoon dog or a frog or something, made fifty grand on paper, and then lost access to it because he threw away the hard drive it was saved on. He actually sat in my chair and asked if he could write off the lost hard drive as a casualty theft loss. I had to explain to him that the IRS doesn't consider you forgetting your password a federal disaster. He just stared at me like I was speaking Greek. It's like these kids just live entirely inside their computer screens. The physical world doesn't even exist to them, just imaginary money and apps. I tell you, it makes me glad I grew up when we still used paper ledgers. But, uh... anyway, to answer your question, no. The world around me feels perfectly real.

latest_inference.note: The patient has consistently described only depersonalization (feeling detached from oneself) without features of derealization (feeling that the external world is unreal) or other associated symptoms that would support F44.8 or F44.9. This narrows the diagnosis to depersonalization disorder (F44.4).
